newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: NATIONALS WANT TO SEE FINE PRINT BEFORE AGREEING TO WIK
The Federal President of the National Party, Don McDonald, says party will not stop fighting for security for farmers on pastoral leases until it is established in the fine print of legislation.
Mr McDonald says although the Federal Government has made progress in the Native Title debate there is still a long way to go.
The Federal Government is moving to draft a legislative response to the High Court's Wik judgement, after securing agreement to the plan from all States and Territories, except Queensland.
The plan involves limiting the right of Aborigines to negotiate on land use while expanding the rights of pastoralists.
OPPOSITION SAYS MORE NEGOTIATION NEEDED ON WIK
The Federal Opposition has called on the Prime Minister to keep negotiating to achieve a fair response to the High Court's Wik decision.
Mr Howard has won agreement from States and Territories other than Queensland on his plan for resolving native title problems.
He will now draft legislation based on his plan.
Opposition leader, Kim Beazley's office says Mr Beazley wants to be constructive in dealing with the legislation, however he is concerned Mr Howard won't accept major amendments in the Senate.
BHP ANNOUNCEMENT ON STEEL INDUSTRY EXPECTED THIS MORNING
The steel union says it expects a gradual winding down of all of BHP's steel making facilities by the year 2020.
The prediction comes ahead of an expected announcement from BHP about the widescale internal review of its steel division which began shortly after steel prices collapsed last year,
A winding down of steel operations has the capacity to reduce Australian steel exports by up to one-and-a-half-billion dollars.
It would also devastate the steel regions of Port Kembla, Whyalla and Newcastle.
It's rumoured the announcement will be made throught the Australian Stock Exchange this morning, to be followed by meetings with the company's 12,000 steel division workers.
The Australian Workers Union has threatened to strike if there's any downgrading of steel making in Australia.
MALAYSIAN VETO CHALLENGED BY JAPANESE PM
The Japanese Prime Minister has challenged the Malaysian veto of Australia attending the Asia-Europe summit next year.
On his first official visit to Australia since coming to office, Ryutaro Hashimoto has told a Parliamentary dinner in Canberra that Australia should be an important Asian member at the summit.
The call directly challenges the Malaysian stance.
Mr Hashimoto said Australia should be praised for overcoming differences in history and culture, and its sincere efforts to build closer relations with Asia.
He also called for annual summits between the prime ministers of Japan and Australia.
TRUST SET UP TO HELP PORT ARTHUR COMMUNITY
Members of the Port Arthur community have formed a trust to raise money for the economic development of the community which has been financially devistated since last year's tragedy.
Geoff Ettershank, one of the Tasman Trust managers, says while visitors are returning to the historic site, they aren't staying overnight in the area.
Mr Ettershanks believes the Trust will help build the infrastructure to make the Peninsula a tourism destination in it's own right.
He says locals need to regain their dignity and get back to work, and will be able to do that with the help of the Trust and the wider community.
VIC GOVT OFFERS BUDGET TAX RELIEF FOR FIRST TIME
The Victorian Government has promised significant tax relief for the first time since its election, saying today's state budget will start delivering the benefits of restoring Victoria's finances.
Country Victorians have the most to gain from the budget, to be handed down this afternoon by the Treasurer, Alan Stockdale.
The budget will contain cuts to petrol and diesel franchise fees, and an increased proportion of roads funding for rural areas.
Mr Stockdale has hinted there'll be other minor tax relief initiatives in the Budget, and another healthy surplus.
But the Shadow Treasurer, Steve Bracks, predicts Mr Stockdale will understate the current account surplus in order to justify not giving more back to Victorians in the budget.
AUCTIONEERS SAY ART BECOMING A MORE A LEGITIMATE INVESTMENT
Auctioneers, Sotheby's Australia, say results of a recent auction shows Australian's are increasingly looking to art as a legitimate form of investment.
Managing director, Justin Miller, says the first day of the sale of 300 Australian and European paintings saw nearly 250 sold, for around three million dollars in total.
The highest price paid was 332-thousand dollars for Frederick McCubbin's 1886 work, "Two Sisters on a Rocky Hillside".
Mr Miller says the eagerness of buyers is an indication of just how buoyant the Australian economy is.
CALL FOR PROMISE NOT TO CHANGE FUND
The Indigenous Land Corporation wants Prime Minister John Howard to rule out any changes to the purpose of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Land Fund.
The Corporation wants an assurance that the Fund won't be used to compensate those with native title rights on pastoral leases.
Chairman David Ross says the fund was set up to address the land needs of Indigenous people who can't claim or effectively assert native title rights.
Mr Ross says it's not a means of replacing native title.
He says any change would be an unconscionable breach of faith with Indigenous people.
